prime.problem: An edge isn't enough: you also have to size the bet. Maximizing expected wealth says stake everything, and it goes broke almost surely; staking too much of a winning bet (twice Kelly on a 60/40 coin) shrinks the typical bankroll even though you win 60% of the time.
prime.fits: Last card of the portfolio part. It uses the returns card's idea that compounding follows the average log return, and the Sharpe card's point that leverage changes return and risk together. The random-walk card then shows the fixed-stake version of the same game.
expect: growth rate g(f) = p ln(1+bf) + q ln(1−f)
prime.goal: Derive and compute the Kelly fraction, explain why maximizing expected log wealth (not expected wealth) is the right target for repeated bets, and argue for betting less than Kelly when p is uncertain.

attend: Why does maximizing expected wealth recommend staking everything, and what does that do to the typical gambler?
Why is the median wealth after n bets e<sup>n·g(f)</sup>, and what does that say about which quantity to maximize?
Why is the growth curve flat at the top but steep past f*?
Why does 2× Kelly land near zero growth, in terms of the returns card's volatility drag?
What happens to a full-Kelly bettor who believes p = 0.6 when the truth is 0.55?

must: Wealth is reinvested → it multiplies bet by bet → the log of wealth is a sum → by the law of large numbers the typical path grows at E[log return] = g(f) → maximize g, not E[wealth]
g(f) = p ln(1+bf) + q ln(1−f) → set g′ = 0 → f* = p − q/b (edge / odds) → 60/40 even money: f* = 0.2, g = 0.02014, about 2% a bet

Staking f raises the mean return linearly but the variance with f² → g ≈ edge·f − (variance)/2 → a parabola peaking at f* and back to 0 near 2f* (0.389 here) → overbetting costs far more than underbetting, and 2× Kelly has median wealth 0.0866 after 1,000 bets

Kelly assumes you know p → overestimating p pushes f past the true f* → you can land on the negative side of the curve (believed 0.6, true 0.55 → g = −0.00014) → half Kelly keeps about ¾ of the growth and much less drawdown, so it's the practical default
elevated: Stakes are a fraction of current wealth → a loss shrinks the next stake → you can never hit exactly 0 → fixed-dollar staking lacks this protection and doesn't compound (41 vs 5.56 × 10⁸ after 1,000 bets)

compress.prompt: Sketch g(f) for the 60/40 coin with f*, half Kelly and 2× Kelly marked, and write the chain from "reinvested wealth" to "maximize expected log" in one line of arrows.
checklist: reinvesting makes wealth multiply, so logs add and the median path grows at g(f)
the curve is flat near f* and steep past it: overbetting is the expensive mistake
g hits zero near 2f*, and wealth shrinks beyond
uncertainty about p is the reason to bet half Kelly

retrieve.q: Explain why "maximize expected wealth" and "maximize expected log wealth" give such different stakes on a repeated favourable bet.
answer: expected wealth is driven by rare, huge winning paths; all-in gives E[W] = 1.2¹⁰⁰⁰ but survival 0.6¹⁰⁰⁰
the typical (median) path grows at E[log return]
maximizing the log protects the typical path and never risks ruin

retrieve.q: Walk through f* and g(f*) for a 55/45 even-money bet, and then g at double that stake.
answer: at f = 0.2: g = −0.00014, just below zero (the zero crossing is at about 0.199)

retrieve.q: Your model says p = 0.6 but you're unsure it isn't 0.55. Compare full Kelly and half Kelly under each truth, and pick one.
answer: truth 0.55: full (0.2) gives −0.00014; half (0.1) gives +0.00501, the true maximum
half Kelly loses a quarter of the growth in the good case and avoids losing money in the bad one: pick half

compare.q: Gambler's ruin bets a fixed $1; Kelly bets a fixed fraction. What does each assume about stake size, and why does one risk ruin and the other never does?
answer: ruin: the stake doesn't shrink as the bankroll shrinks, so a run of losses reaches 0
Kelly: the stake is a fraction of current wealth, so losses shrink the next bet and wealth stays above 0
with a negative edge, the fixed-stake card's advice (bold play) is the opposite: fewer, bigger bets
Kelly with a negative edge says f* < 0: don't bet

compare.q: The EV card prices games at their expected value; this card refuses to maximize expected wealth. When is expected value the right criterion and when is it log?
answer: EV is right for a risk-neutral player who can repeat small bets or hedge them away
when you reinvest a bankroll, outcomes multiply and log wealth is what adds
the EV card's own caveat, $1M a pip, is the Kelly point: bet size relative to bankroll matters

predict.q: A bet pays 2 to 1 and you win 40% of the time. Is it worth betting, and if so, what fraction? Then: what is g at twice that fraction? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Edge = 2 × 0.4 − 0.6 = 0.2 > 0, so yes. f* = p − q/b = 0.4 − 0.6/2 = 0.10, with g = 0.4 ln 1.2 + 0.6 ln 0.9 = 0.00971 per bet. At 0.2, g = 0.4 ln 1.4 + 0.6 ln 0.8 = +0.00070: still barely positive, because with b = 2 the curve is not symmetric around f*. The "2× Kelly ≈ zero" rule is only exact for the parabola approximation.

apply.task: Change the card's simulate() to compare f = 0.05, 0.10 and 0.20 on a 55/45 even-money coin for 1,000 bets and 2,001 paths. Before running, predict the median-wealth ranking from g(f). Then add a fixed-dollar strategy that stakes 0.1 of starting wealth each bet and stops at 0.
apply.done: Your predicted and simulated medians agree in order: f = 0.10 (g = 0.00501, median ≈ e<sup>5.0</sup>) beats 0.05 (g = 0.00375) and 0.20 (g = −0.00014, median just under 1). You can explain in one sentence why the fixed-dollar strategy's median gain grows only linearly.
apply.hint: The median path has exactly 550 wins, so its wealth is (1 + f)<sup>550</sup>(1 − f)<sup>450</sup> = e<sup>1000·g(f)</sup>.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether the 2:1 bet at 2f* still grows?
